Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us The Legacy of Slavery As the United States expanded from 13 colonies, the debates over chattel slavery grew—some states came to abolish it, while others refused to untangle their political, economic, and social life from the institution. With the outbreak of the Civil War in 1861, enslaved African Americans saw the war as opportunity to emancipate themselves. When President Lincoln authorized the Emancipation Proclamation, formerly enslaved African American men joined the Union army to fight for the full emancipation of their race. The conclusion of the war in Union victory and the ratification of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the US Constitution brought African Americans closer than they ever had been to full citizenship. Nevertheless, the struggle for equality continued. Through our historical resources, the National Park Service tells these stories of African-American perseverance in the face of great adversity. Mission CDC's environmental microbiology and engineering laboratories conduct research to better understand infectious germs present in outdoor or indoor environments. HHCB is a synthetic musk used widely in fragrances and in household products such as detergents, cleaners, and air fresheners. Because this chemical is used so broadly, EPA’s review needs to reflect the full body of available science and give the public an opportunity to review the same information EPA used in its draft assessment. EPA Finalizes Updates to Formaldehyde Emission Standards, Adds New Quality Control Test Method for Composite Wood Products Released October 23, 2026 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is adding a new quality control test method for measuring formaldehyde air emissions from composite wood products as part of routine updates to its Formaldehyde Emission Standards for Composite Wood Products under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA). Formaldehyde is a component of resins and adhesives used to make composite wood products such as plywood, particleboard, and medium-density fiberboard, which are found in furniture, cabinets, flooring, and building materials. It can be released into indoor air from these products. The Formaldehyde Standards for Composite Wood Products Act of 2010 directed EPA to set emission limits for these products to reduce exposure and protect public health. Spent the morning with the Bicycle wiki page and a 300-post thread about access=dismount, and the same thing kept coming up: our cycling data is really good at describing the road, and a bit less good at describing the person on the bike. We tag the surface, the separation, the access. But the thing that decides whether I actually ride a route is rain, fatigue, and whether I trust the stretch where the cycle lane ends and the traffic doesn’t slow down. None of that is in the data, and it’s the part that matters on a Tuesday morning when it’s pouring. I keep coming back to the idea that the gap between “legal to ride” and “would actually ride” is where the interesting mapping is. Maybe that’s a project for a quieter evening. March 19, 2025 Estimates: Burden of Foodborne Illness in the United States What to know Foodborne illness estimates can serve as a foundation for future public health action. CDC estimated the average number of U.S. foodborne illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths in 2019 caused by seven major pathogens. Six of these pathogens caused 9.9 million domestically acquired foodborne illnesses. Illnesses caused by all seven pathogens resulted in 53,300 hospitalizations and 931 deaths. Why do we estimate? Knowing how many foodborne illnesses occur – or the burden of disease – provides us with a better understanding of an important public health problem. Surveillance systems and surveys provide vital information about the burden of foodborne illness in the United States, but they do not capture every illness. pages.description: Estonia is the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine.
pages.text: Estonia latest country to ban Russian athletes as backlash intensifies - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Estonia shares a border with Russia By Dan Roan Sports editor Published 13 November 2026 Estonia has become the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine. It comes after Norway, Finland and Canada made similar announcements. The moves come amid a mounting backlash over the reinstatement of athletes from Russia and Belarus. In September, the International Ski Federation (FIS) relaxed its rules, saying competitors from the two countries would be granted access to its events "provided that they sign a declaration of neutrality". They had previously faced more stringent background checks on any voluntary link or paid duty with the military. Participation remains limited to individual events, with athletes banned from displaying national symbols such as flags, anthems or uniforms. However, it has now emerged that Estonia's government has written to the FIS, claiming that allowing entry to competitors from Russia and Belarus would undermine the country's support of Ukraine, and present an opportunity for propaganda. It said a ban issued in 2022 will be maintained. In a statement issued to BBC Sport, the FIS said it "is committed to offering full support to athletes, national ski associations and local organisers - with most of which we have a long-standing relationship - in the process of navigating what we know to be a very complex situation. Westend61, Getty Images By Sean Newsom Published June 10, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). A multi-day hike is a very particular kind of challenge. The demands on mind and body layer up day after day and, to confront them in the best possible shape, it’s important to get proper rest each night. This is more easily done with a roof over your head than the flapping canvas of a tent and, in some protected landscapes, wild camping is forbidden. Happily, Europe is well-equipped with mountain refuges, pilgrim hostels and path-adjacent hotels. Many stand-out stays are in the Alps — but, as you’ll see from our guide, not all. Here lie the tallest cliffs and the most unspoilt landscapes, as well as deep layers of culture and history. It’s an extraordinary place to connect with the beauty and reliance nature has to offer.” Newcomers among the three million visitors who pass through each year are often surprised by the abrupt transition between the park’s Mojave and Colorado deserts. Climbers rest on top of a rock before rappelling back to the valley floor in Joshua Tree National Park. Ben Horton, Nat Geo Image Collection The Mojave or “High Desert” claims the park’s western half, where giant branching yuccas thrive on sandy plains studded by massive granite monoliths and rock piles. These are among the most intriguing and photogenic geological phenomena found in California’s many desert regions. The Colorado or “Low Desert” thrives on the park’s gently declining eastern flank, where temperatures are usually higher. It often seems sparse and forbidding. Yet here and there are colorful desert “gardens” of flowering ocotillo and cholla cactus. Dozens of trails are open to hiking, biking, and horseback riding, and the stony terrain makes it one of America’s rock climbing meccas. pages.text: Everything you should know about Death Valley National Park | National Geographic TRAVEL Everything you should know about Death Valley National Park A hiker climbs a hill to witness the iridescent sunset in Death Valley National Park. Alex Treadway/National Geographic Image Collection By Susan B. Barnes Last updated July 14, 2026 • 20 min read Spanning an impressive 3.4 million acres across California and Nevada , Death Valley National Park is the largest national park in the lower 48 states, approximately the size of Connecticut . Though its name can be off-putting and it’s known as the driest, hottest, and lowest national park in the U.S., Death Valley is an interesting and diverse landscape that’s home to wildlife, wildflowers, and centuries of human history. Long before it became a national park, the land that comprises Death Valley was home to the Timbisha Shoshone people, who lived here for more than 1,000 years. They found everything they needed to survive on the land, from hunting to harvesting pinyon pine nuts and mesquite beans. In the second half of the 1800s, those heading west to California to seek their fortune came upon Death Valley; mining towns and borax factories popped up. One of those companies, the Pacific Coast Borax Company, saw the potential of tourism in Death Valley and began campaigning to have the area designated as a national park in the mid-1920s. President Herbert Hoover designated Death Valley a national monument in 1933; it was declared a national park by Congress in 1994. ( Avoid the crowds at the 10 least-visited U.S. national parks .) pages.text: Everything you should know about Voyageurs National Park | National Geographic TRAVEL Everything you should know about Voyageurs National Park This remote northern wilderness is an ethereal land of lakes and star-filled skies—and one of America’s most underrated national parks. For the best paddleboarding, visitors at Voyageurs National Park should head to the sheltered bays of the four major interconnected lakes: Rainy, Kabetogama, Namakan, and Sandy Point. Per Breiehagen, Getty Images By Miles Griffis Last updated May 12, 2026 • 14 min read Hugging the Canadian border, Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park is a floating landscape of glacially carved lakes fringed with thick boreal forests. The park was named for the French Canadian fur traders who paddled enormous birch and cedar canoes through the region in the 1800s. Today, “Voyageurs [National Park] offers you a view to the past to see the natural shoreline of this amazing lake country,” says Christina Hausman Rhode, the executive director of the nonprofit Voyageurs Conservancy . Though the park commemorates these hardy woodsmen, the region’s first stewards were the ancestors of the Bois Forte Chippewa (Ojibwe), who entered the area more than 10,000 years ago. They first paddled the three stately lakes—Kabetogama, Rainy, and Namakan—that circle the remote Kabetogama Peninsula, where packs of eastern gray wolves thrive. Evidential statistics is the math that helps forensic scientists understand the degree of confidence after their measurement is made. Experts call this uncertainty . Evaluating uncertainty provides essential context for interpreting results. This information helps criminal justice professionals understand the strengths and limitations of their evidence. What is NIST’s Role? Our experts: Address statistical challenges that affect how evidence is evaluated, interpreted and communicated across multiple forensic fields. Develop tools and algorithms to help forensic scientists assess uncertainty and evaluate their methods. Provide statistical support to criminal justice professionals, connecting mathematical theory to everyday forensic science practice. pages.text: Exclusive: There’s a new T. rex in town—and this giant beast ruled the seas | National Geographic SCIENCE Exclusive: There’s a new T. rex in town—and this giant beast ruled the seas Equipped with powerful jaws and finely serrated teeth, paleontologists say the 43-foot-long prehistoric marine reptile deserves the name Tylosaurus rex. After remeasuring dozens of mosasaur specimens across multiple museums, paleontologists discovered a previously unknown species of mosasaur, Tylosaurus rex, that reigned supreme 80 million years ago, seen here in an artist's reconstruction. Courtesy Alderon Games, Path of Titans/AMNH By Asher Elbein Published May 21, 2026 What do you call a massive prehistoric reptilian tyrant, with large, powerful jaws and sharp serrated teeth? If you said Tyrannosaurus rex , that’s understandable: it’s the most famous dinosaurian predator ever. But this mystery beast swam the ocean depths, where no land-stalking Tyrannosaurus ever dove. What would you call that? If you said “ T. rex,” you’d be correct! Paleontologists have discovered an enormous new species of Tylosaurus , a sea lizard belonging to the mosasaur family. Measuring up to 43 feet long—the size of a humpback whale—this 80-million-year-old apex predator is among the biggest known mosasaurs. They named it Tylosaurus rex, or “king of the Tylosaurs,” a name that comes with an iconic abbreviation. “If any animal deserves it, it’s this animal,” says Amelia Zietlow , a paleontologist previously at the American Museum of Natural History in New York and now at the History Museum at the Castle in Wisconsin.

Existing Chemical Exposure Limits under TSCA The Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) gives EPA the authority to take action to address unreasonable risks to public health or the environment from chemicals currently on the market. Where a chemical presents an unreasonable risk to human health in the workplace, EPA may develop an occupational exposure limit, known as an Existing Chemical Exposure Limit (ECEL), as part of a chemical management program to address worker risk. On this page: What is an Existing Chemical Exposure Limit (ECEL)? Why would EPA require an Existing Chemical Exposure Limit (ECEL)? On other pages: List of Final and Proposed Existing Chemical Exposure Limits (ECELs) under TSCA New Chemical Exposure Limits (NCELs) What is an Existing Chemical Exposure Limit (ECEL)? An Existing Chemical Exposure Limit (ECEL) is a regulatory occupational exposure limit (OEL) set by EPA to limit inhalation risks to workers exposed to certain chemicals in a workplace. The ECEL is a maximum average airborne concentration of the chemical that someone can be exposed to in the workplace without experiencing unreasonable risk from inhalation exposure to the chemical.
